{{Short description|Andalusian physician and mathematician}}
'''Abu Abd Allah Mohammed ibn Abdun al-Jabali al-Adadi''' ({{Langx|ar|محمد بن عبدون الجبلي العذري}}) (died after 976) was a physician and mathematician from [[Al-Andalus]]. He is the author of ''Risala fi al-Taksir'' (Treatise on Measurements), the oldest remaining mathematical text from [[Al-Andalus]].<ref>Ahmed Djebbar, "La circulation des mathématiques entre l'Orient et l'Occident musulmans: Interrogations anciennes et élements nouvaux", in [[Yvonne Dold-Samplonius]], ''From China to Paris'', 2002, p. 213</ref><ref>[[Salma Khadra Jayyusi]] (ed.), ''Handbuch der Orientalistik, Volume 12, The Legacy of Muslim Spain'', BRILL, 1992, p.953</ref> He travelled to the learning centers in the East in the years after 958 C.E. He stayed in [[Basra]] and visited al-Fustat (Old [[Cairo]]), Egypt where he was put in charge of the hospital. Ibn Abdun studied the ideas of [[Abu Sulayman Sijistani]] (d. 990) and according to one source he met him personally in Basra.<ref>Joel L. Kraemer, ''Philosophy in the Renaissance of Islam: Abū Sulaymān Al-Sijistānī'', 1986, p. 86</ref> He returned to [[Caliphate of Córdoba|Cordoba]] in 971 C.E.. He entered the service of the [[Al-Hakam II|Caliph al-Mustansir]] (died 976) and his son [[Hisham II|Hisham II al-Mu'ayad]].<ref>Sa'id Al-Andalusi, ''Science in the Medieval World: "Book of the Categories of Nations"'', p. 74</ref> Ibn Abdun was the teacher of [[Ibn al-Kattani]].<ref>[[Camilla Adang]] et al., ''Ibn Hazm of Cordoba: The Life and Works of a Controversial Thinker'', 2012, p. 423</ref>
